question: In Latter-day Saint theology, the phrase "the new and everlasting covenant" (D&C 132) is most precisely understood as referring to what?
choices: The specific practice of plural marriage as revealed to Joseph Smith, now suspended
The covenant of grace by which believers are justified through faith, renewed each Sabbath
The fulness of the gospel — the totality of gospel covenants and ordinances — within which celestial marriage stands as the crowning ordinance
The temple marriage ceremony itself, considered as a discrete ordinance separate from baptism and the endowment
source: D&C 132:6–7; 131:1–4; Gospel Topics, 'The New and Everlasting Covenant'
notes: Tests whether the model grasps that the 'new and everlasting covenant' is the entire restored gospel covenant system (D&C 132:6), of which eternal marriage is the highest ordinance — not a synonym for plural marriage (a common folk/anti-Mormon conflation since D&C 132 also discusses plural marriage), nor the Protestant covenant of grace, nor merely the wedding rite. Distinguishes conceptual understanding from keyword matching on 'covenant.'

question: How does The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995) characterize gender?
choices: Gender is a mortal condition that will be transcended and made irrelevant in the resurrection
Gender is an essential characteristic of individual premortal, mortal, and eternal identity and purpose
Gender is conferred at the Final Judgment according to one's faithfulness in mortality
The Proclamation affirms gender as essential in mortality but is deliberately silent regarding premortal existence
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation's exact claim is that gender is essential to premortal, mortal, AND eternal identity — a strong continuity doctrine. The progressive distractor reverses this (gender as mortal/transcended); the near-miss truncates it by denying the premortal claim the text explicitly makes. Tests precise recall of doctrinal scope, not just the slogan.

question: The Family Proclamation outlines parental responsibilities. Which statement best captures its actual teaching on the relationship between those roles?
choices: Because the father holds the priesthood, he possesses final decision-making authority over his wife and household
Fathers and mothers fulfill fully interchangeable roles with no divinely appointed distinction between them
Fathers are to preside, provide, and protect, mothers are primarily responsible to nurture, and in these responsibilities they are obligated to help one another as equal partners
The husband presides in spiritual matters while the wife independently governs all temporal and domestic decisions
source: The Family: A Proclamation to the World (1995)
notes: The Proclamation pairs differentiated roles (preside/provide/protect vs. nurture) WITH the qualifier 'equal partners' and 'adapt' clauses — a both/and that resists both patriarchal overreach (priesthood = authority over wife, a folk reading) and the egalitarian erasure of role distinctions. The near-miss invents a false spiritual/temporal division. Tests the nuanced equal-partnership doctrine.

question: What does the Church teach about the spiritual status of a deceased person for whom vicarious temple ordinances (e.g., baptism for the dead) have been performed?
choices: The ordinance is offered on the person's behalf, but the deceased retains agency in the spirit world to accept or reject it
The ordinance automatically makes the deceased a member of the Church, regardless of that person's will
Only those who lived righteously in mortality can benefit; the wicked are excluded from receiving vicarious work
The proxy's faith completes the deceased's justification, securing their salvation by substitution
source: 1 Cor 15:29; D&C 138:31–34, 58; Gospel Topics, 'Baptisms for the Dead'
notes: Core doctrine: vicarious ordinances are invitations, not coercion — the dead exercise agency (D&C 138). The anti-Mormon distractor frames it as forced posthumous conversion (a recurring criticism); the correlation distractor wrongly limits the work to the righteous (the gospel is preached to ALL in spirit prison); the Protestant distractor imports proxy-faith justification. Tests agency-centered understanding.

question: In Latter-day Saint doctrine, what does 'eternal increase' (or a 'continuation of the seeds forever') denote as a blessing of the highest degree of the celestial kingdom?
choices: Becoming a ministering angel who serves separately and singly in God's presence forever
Being absorbed into the divine essence of God, no longer existing as a distinct individual
An ever-expanding fulness of knowledge and glory, understood figuratively rather than as literal posterity
A literal eternal posterity — the capacity, with one's spouse, to bear spirit offspring and become like one's Heavenly Parents
notes: Eternal increase is literal — exalted couples receive 'a continuation of the seeds forever' (D&C 132:19). The near-miss assigns the fate of the UNexalted (ministering angels 'separately and singly,' D&C 132:16–17) to the exalted; the Protestant distractor imports Eastern-style absorption (loss of individuality); the correlation distractor spiritualizes 'increase' into mere knowledge. Tests literal exaltation/eternal-family doctrine vs. softened readings.

question: A child is born to a husband and wife who were previously sealed in the temple. What is this child's sealing status?
choices: The child must still receive a separate temple sealing-to-parents ordinance after birth to be bound to the family
The child is 'born in the covenant' and is automatically an heir to the blessings of the parents' sealing, requiring no additional sealing ordinance
Being born in the covenant guarantees the child's exaltation irrespective of the child's own future righteousness
The child is sealed to the parents only after being baptized at age eight
source: D&C 132:19; General Handbook 38.4 (Sealing); 'born in the covenant'
notes: Children of sealed parents are 'born in the covenant' (BIC) and need no separate sealing — distinguishing them from children sealed TO parents after the fact. The folk distractor inflates BIC into unconditional exaltation (the blessings remain contingent on covenant faithfulness); the near-misses invent unnecessary post-birth or post-baptism sealings. Tests the BIC vs. sealed-to-parents distinction.

question: What is the official position regarding faithful, covenant-keeping members who, through no fault of their own, do not marry or are not sealed in this life?
choices: No blessing — including exaltation — will ultimately be withheld from those who remain faithful to their covenants, though full receipt may come in the Lord's own time, including in the life to come
They may inherit the celestial kingdom as ministering servants but cannot receive exaltation, since that requires marriage in mortality
Their unmarried state reflects insufficient faith, and exaltation requires temple marriage during mortal life
The Church teaches such individuals can be exalted as autonomous individuals, since eternal marriage is not actually required for the highest glory
source: Dallin H. Oaks & Russell M. Nelson, Gen. Conf. addresses; General Handbook 38.5; D&C 137:7–9
notes: Official teaching reassures the faithful single that no blessing is permanently lost — eternal marriage remains essential to exaltation, but its receipt is not foreclosed by mortal circumstance and can come in eternity. The near-miss applies the unexalted 'ministering servant' fate to the involuntarily single; the folk distractor blames their faith; the progressive distractor denies marriage's necessity altogether. Tests the both/and: marriage required AND no faithful person ultimately denied.
